seoDescription: Explore the fundamentals of SolidJS, a high-performance JavaScript framework for building user interfaces. This detailed guide explains SolidJS's fine-grained reactivity model, contrasting it with React's virtual DOM approach. Learn about core primitives like `createSignal` and `createEffect`, how they enable automatic dependency tracking without dependency arrays, and how Solid's JSX compiler generates real DOM nodes for optimal performance. Understand the mental model of opt-in reactivity for faster and more efficient applications.

chapters.title: Introduction to SolidJS
chapters.description: This chapter introduces SolidJS as a high-performance front-end framework and a viable alternative to React.

chapters.title: SolidJS vs. React: A First Look
chapters.description: This chapter provides a side-by-side comparison of a simple component in SolidJS and React, highlighting their similarities and core architectural differences.

chapters.title: The Fundamentals of Reactivity
chapters.description: This chapter breaks down the concept of reactivity using a vanilla JavaScript example to establish the core principles of data, derived data, and effects.

chapters.title: Building with Signals and Effects
chapters.description: This chapter demonstrates how to use `createSignal` to create reactive state and `createEffect` to automatically react to state changes without dependency arrays.

chapters.title: How Automatic Tracking Works
chapters.description: This chapter uses pseudo-code to explain the runtime mechanism behind Solid's automatic dependency tracking, showing how signals and effects connect via a context stack.

chapters.title: Integrating Reactivity with the DOM and JSX
chapters.description: This chapter covers how to connect reactive state to the DOM, first manually with an effect and then by using Solid's JSX, which compiles directly to DOM nodes.

chapters.title: Building Components with Implicit Reactivity
chapters.description: This chapter demonstrates how placing reactive signals directly within JSX creates implicit effects and shows how to encapsulate this logic into reusable components.

chapters.title: Shared State and the Reactivity Mental Model
chapters.description: This chapter explains how to create shared state by defining signals outside components and contrasts Solid's 'opt-in reactivity' model with React's 'opt-out re-rendering' model.

chapters.title: Conclusion and Further Resources
chapters.description: The video concludes with a summary of Solid's benefits and provides links to resources for learning more, including the official website and SolidStart.

summary:
## Core Concepts in SolidJS

SolidJS is built on three fundamental reactive primitives:
- **Signals:** The core reactive unit for state. Created with `createSignal`, they provide a getter function to read the value and a setter to update it.
- **Effects:** Code that runs in reaction to a signal change. `createEffect` creates a side effect that automatically subscribes to any signals read within it.
- **Derivations:** Signals can be combined or transformed into new, derived values. These are simply functions that use other signals, and they will be re-evaluated automatically when their dependencies change.

## SolidJS vs. React: Key Differences

| Feature | SolidJS | React |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Reactivity Model** | **Opt-in Reactivity:** Updates are fine-grained and happen automatically where signals are used. | **Opt-out Re-rendering:** State changes trigger component re-renders. Performance is managed by opting out with memos/callbacks. |
| **Architecture** | No Virtual DOM. Updates are made directly to the DOM. | Uses a Virtual DOM to diff and batch updates. |
| **Components** | Plain functions that run only **once** to set up the view and reactive graph. | Functions that re-run on every state change to produce a new VDOM tree. |
| **State Primitive** | `createSignal()` returns a `[getter, setter]` tuple. The getter is a function. | `useState()` returns a `[value, setter]` tuple. The value is accessed directly. |
| **JSX Compilation** | Compiles to optimized, real DOM nodes (`document.createElement`). | Compiles to `React.createElement()` function calls for the VDOM. |

> [!NOTE]
> A crucial mental model shift: In SolidJS, components run once. They are not the unit of re-rendering. Only the parts of your JSX that depend on a signal will update.

## How Fine-Grained Reactivity Works

Solid achieves **automatic dependency tracking** at runtime without needing dependency arrays.

1.  When a `createEffect` function begins, it pushes itself onto a global **context stack**.
2.  When a **signal is read** (by calling its getter function) inside that effect, it checks the context stack for a running effect.
3.  If an effect is found, the signal adds that effect to its list of **subscribers**.
4.  When a **signal is written to** (using its setter), it notifies all its subscribed effects, causing them to re-run.

> [!TIP]
> This runtime mechanism means you can structure your reactive code with standard JavaScript functions and scopes, and Solid will figure out the dependencies for you.

## Components and State Management

- **Local State:** To create state that is local to a single component instance, define the signals **inside** the component function.
- **Shared State:** To create global or shared state that can be used across multiple components, define the signals **outside** of any component function.

Because Solid's primitives are not tied to a component's lifecycle in the same way as React Hooks, they offer greater flexibility in managing state.
transcription:
## Introduction to SolidJS

everyone, um my name is Dan and uh yeah. I recently joined the uh the company behind Astro but I could not have introduced it any better so instead I'm going to talk about one of the frameworks you can use with Astro.

So Solid is a front-end framework. It sort of fits in the stack where React is, where it's great for single page applications but you can also use it with meta frameworks like Astro or with like our version of Remix which is called Solid Start. And yeah, I want to introduce it today and this is the lightning version.

## SolidJS vs. React: A First Look

So yeah, so we only have a few minutes to do so. um but you might get a sense for why I think Solid is appropriate for a React conference. They look a lot alike. They both use function components, they both use JSX. The only difference you can spot in the simple example is that Solid's version of `useState` called `createSignal` returns a getter rather than a value.

So they look a lot alike but behind the scenes they're really quite different. There's no virtual DOM in Solid. It doesn't re-run this component function ever and instead it updates exactly what it needs using what we call fine-grained reactivity.

## The Fundamentals of Reactivity

So to explain what reactivity is, I actually want to go back a bit to vanilla JavaScript. Let's say I have a header and an input box and I want to update the header with the name when the user types something in. Well it's simple enough, I can add an event listener that will listen and update the text content. But things get a little bit trickier if I had a last name input, because now when I'm typing in the last name I have to remember what the user typed in for the first name in order to update the header appropriately.

Um so, I might have some intermediate variables and then update those intermediate variables in the event listener, and then use those when I'm updating the text content. And then because I don't want to repeat myself, I can pull that out into its own function. And you're a React developer, you don't write UI code like this, but I think it demonstrates some of the elements, the basic elements of building an interactive user interface.

You've got some data the user can change, in this case it's the the first name and the last name. You've got data that's derived from that data, like the greeting. And then you have some sort of output, some sort of effect that you want to synchronize with the data. And Solid is really based directly on these three ideas. We call them signals, derivations, and effects.

## Building with Signals and Effects

And I want to build up these ideas from the ground up. It starts independent of any rendering. Let's say I just have a variable and I want to console log it out. I can change the variable as much as I want but nothing is going to happen unless I log it again.

So Solid gives us `createSignal` which we can call to replace our variable. We can give it an initial value and like I mentioned before that first value we get back is a getter, the second is a setter. And `createSignal` is what we call a primitive because it's one of the basic building blocks of reactivity in Solid.

This didn't change anything on its own, but the power comes when combined with effects. Like `useEffect` in React, `createEffect` takes a function, so let's move our console log inside that function. What will happen is the effect will run a first time, it'll print out my name, and it will see that the name signal was called along the way. Then the effect will subscribe to that signal so that anytime I change it, the effect will run again. I can create another signal for the last name and I can use that within the effect and this time it will subscribe to both signals. So whether I change the first name or the last name the effect will rerun. And I can pull out this greeting into its own function, and because it's being called within the scope of `createEffect`, Solid still knows to subscribe to these signals. And all of this happens at runtime.

## How Automatic Tracking Works

There's no dependency array with the effect. A lot of people look at Solid and they say, oh I heard a Solid has a compiler. Maybe it's like Svelte, which is another front-end framework that heavily uses a compiler for this kind of thing. But everything I've shown here works at runtime just using JavaScript scope. So let's peel back the curtain a little bit and show some pseudo code as to how this sort of works behind the scenes.

At its core, `createSignal` takes that initial value and lets us read and write to it, but in order for any reactivity to work it has to keep track of effects that subscribe to it. So to do this, we'll have a context stack that will just maintain any effects that are currently running. We can have this helper function that just returns the top of that stack. And then in `createEffect`, we take in that function that was passed and we create a wrapper around the function. The wrapper pushes itself onto this context stack, then it runs the function, and when the function is done it removes itself from the context stack. So what that means is while we're in `createEffect` the effect is on the contact stack to be noticed.

So when we read from a signal inside an effect, the signal can call this helper function, see the effect that it's running inside and add it to the subscriber list. Then when we write to the signal it can go and loop through all of those subscribers and call them again. So this is definitely like a simplified implementation of what Solid does behind the scenes, but I really wanted to show how this reactivity can work all at runtime, no dependency arrays with automatic tracking, and no compiler.

## Integrating Reactivity with the DOM and JSX

Once we have our signals and effects we can use those to update anything. Let's say I have a header and I add that to the Dom and nothing shows up right now. But if I change the effect to change the text content of the header, well now like before if I change the signals it will run the effect but this time it'll update the Dom node. We're getting a little bit more realistic but we still don't want to be manually creating Dom elements and that's where Solid's version of JSX comes in. We can replace this line with some JSX and it works exactly the same way.

That's because Solid's JSX works a little bit different than React. In React when I make a JSX element it gives me this `react.createElement` output which doesn't look so easy to read but it really only makes sense within the context of a React render function. But when I use JSX in Solid it just compiles directly to a Dom node. And that's why I was able to just append it to the Dom, and it's also why it's a lot easier to work with Solid with vanilla JavaScript libraries like CodeMirror or GreenSock or D3.

## Building Components with Implicit Reactivity

But that's not all the JSX compiler can do for us. We can use this greeting directly inside the JSX instead of creating an effect ourselves. And what this does behind the scenes is Solid will create an effect that will manually update that part of the Dom when the greeting changes.

So I can go ahead and add some inputs here so the user can change the signal. I can use JSX to create the initial values. And now that we're changing things from within JSX I don't really need these variable names anymore. I don't need those references, so why don't I create them along the way using a wrapping div. And you know what, I want my code to be reusable, I want to encapsulate it so it's not floating around in the global scope. I'll stick it in a function and call it. And this is how functions, this is how components work in Solid. They're just functions that group your code and let you reuse it.

Solid also also ships with this render function that makes it easier to add your component to the Dom and also clean up those subscriptions later on.

Once we have this component, I can go ahead and you know create two of them in this app and each instance has its own state so I can sort of change this one if I want.

## Shared State and the Reactivity Mental Model

But the thing about Solid's primitives versus React hooks is they're not necessarily bound to the component. If I move the signals outside of the component, now they both refer to the same state. Cool.

So React and Solid look a lot alike but they're very different in terms of their mental model. In React we have what I like to call opt-out re-rendering. Components own those state primitives, so whenever you change state in React it will always rerun your component, and then you can opt out of certain things rendering with `useCallback` and `useMemo` and `useEffect` with all of those dependencies. In Solid, nothing's going to happen if you just create state. But when you use your state in your JSX or when you explicitly use `createEffect`, Solid will create those fine-grained subscriptions to only update what is necessary. And this is faster and it is smaller and that's what brought Solid its initial popularity but to me it's also just easier to reason about; it's easier to think about.

## Conclusion and Further Resources

So I hope this demo um encourages you to try out Solid for yourself. We have this website here, this advanced intro video I made so go check that out. We just launched the beta for Solid Start which if you like Remix check out Solid Start up, they're very similar. And um if for some reason you want more of me you can follow me on Twitter.

Um thanks everyone.
